VB-GRAMG Act


• The Government of India has notified the Viksit Bharat–
  Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-
  GRAMG) Act, 2025, which will come into force nationwide from 1
  July 2026, replacing the nearly 20-year-old MGNREGA scheme.

• The Act raises the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days
  to 125 days of wage employment per rural household per
  financial year.

• On 11 May 2026, the Ministry of Rural Development formally
  notified that the VB-GRAMG Act will be brought into force with effect
  from 1 July 2026 across all States and Union Territories.

VB-GRAMG Act
MGNREGA –

• Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was
  enacted in 2005 and came into force on 2 February 2006 as the
  world’s largest work guarantee programme.

• The Act was inspired by the Maharashtra Employment
  Guarantee Scheme (MEGS) of 1972, which itself originated as a
  drought relief programme in the early 1970s.

• The Act was structured to be demand-driven: employment was
  provided on demand, and funds were allocated accordingly.

VB-GRAMG Act



• Although the Constitution does not expressly recognise the right to
  work as a fundamental right, Article 41 (Directive Principles)
  directs the State to make effective provision for securing the right to
  work.

• The Supreme Court, in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal
  Corporation (1985) , recognised that the right to livelihood is an
  integral facet of the right to life under Article 21.

VB-GRAMG Act


• MGNREGA guaranteed 100 days of wage employment per
  household per year, with the wage rate linked to the Consumer
  Price Index for Agricultural Labour (CPI-AL).

• The Act provided for an unemployment allowance – if a person
  seeking work was not provided employment within 15 days, the
  state government was required to pay unemployment allowance for
  each day of delay.

• The wage-material ratio mandated that at least 60% of total
  expenditure should be on wages, with material costs limited to
  40%, and contractors were prohibited from executing works under
  the scheme.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Under MGNREGA, the Central Government undertook 100% of the
  wage costs (which constitute the bulk of the expenditure) while
  states contributed 25% of material costs.

• This funding pattern effectively made the Central Government the
  primary financial guarantor of the right to employment, relieving
  states from an open-ended financial burden.

• When states submitted annual work plans based on demand, the
  Centre was obligated to release funds accordingly.

VB-GRAMG Act
Features of New Act –

• With effect from 1 July 2026, the MGNREGA will stand repealed,
  along with all rules, notifications and guidelines issued under it.

• However, existing e-KYC-verified MGNREGA job cards will
  remain valid until new “Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards” are
  issued, ensuring a smooth administrative transition.

• Workers with pending e-KYC verification will not be denied
  employment, and fresh registrations will continue at the gram
  panchayat level.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act provides a statutory guarantee of not less than 125
  days of wage employment per rural household in each financial year
  (Section 5(1)), an increase of 25 days over MGNREGA.

• This period is to be provided during the period outside the
  agricultural pause.

• The guaranteed employment is to be provided to households whose
  adult members volunteer to undertake unskilled manual work,
  with the work linked to durable asset creation.

VB-GRAMG Act


• State governments are empowered to notify an aggregated pause
  period up to 60 days in a financial year during which works under
  the scheme will not be undertaken (Section 6).

• This pause is intended to cover peak agricultural seasons,
  including sowing and harvesting, to facilitate adequate availability of
  agricultural labor.

• The 60-day pause provision has been criticised as
  effectively reducing the effective work guarantee to 65 days,
  because the provision does not require states to compensate for lost
  work days during the pause.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Wages must be paid on a weekly basis or, in any case, within 15
  days of completion of work.

• In case of delay beyond the stipulated period, delay
  compensation shall be payable in accordance with Schedule II of
  the Act, reinforcing wage security and protecting workers from
  delays.

• The unemployment allowance provision (payable if work is not
  provided within 15 days of demand) has been retained from
  MGNREGA, with rates linked to the notified wage rate.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Unlike MGNREGA (where the Centre undertook all wage costs), VB-
  GRAMG will be implemented as a Centrally Sponsored
  Scheme with shared financing between Centre and States.

• The fund-sharing pattern will be 60:40 for all states (Centre 60%,
  State 40%), and 90:10 for North-eastern and Himalayan
  States (Union Territories without legislatures will receive full central
  funding).

• The State Government will continue to pay unemployment
  allowance and compensation, and will also bear any expenditure
  incurred in excess of the normative allocation.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act empowers the Central Government to determine state-wise
  normative allocation for each financial year – a fixed spending
  ceiling.

• Any expenditure incurred by a State in excess of this allocation
  must be borne by the State government itself, converting the
  earlier “open-ended” demand-driven scheme into a budget-capped
  program.

• The parameters for fixing these allocations will be prescribed by the
  Central Government later through Rules.

VB-GRAMG Act

• Wage employment under the Act is explicitly aligned with the creation
  of durable public assets across four priority thematic
  domains (Schedule I):

 ➢ Water security and water-related works (irrigation,
   conservation, ponds)；

 ➢ Core rural infrastructure (roads, bridges, culverts)；

 ➢ Livelihood-related infrastructure (rural haats, storage
   structures, work sheds, livestock shelters)； and

 ➢ Works to mitigate extreme weather events (flood control, soil
   conservation).

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act makes at least one-third participation of
  women mandatory, with special focus on women-headed
  households (through special job cards) and on single women.

• Crèche facilities are to be provided at worksites where five or more
  children under five years accompany working women, and a woman
  worker is to be appointed to care for them.

• One-third representation of women is mandatory in the
  Central Rojgar Guarantee Council and State Rojgar
  Guarantee Councils to be constituted under the Act.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The VB-GRAMG Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16
  December 2025, passed by the Lok Sabha on 18 December, and
  cleared by the Rajya Sabha after midnight on 19 December 2025.

• The Bill received Presidential assent on 21 December 2025,
  with the Act taking effect six months later.

• The entire legislative process was completed in just six days – a
  speed that drew criticism from Opposition leaders, including Punjab
  Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, who accused the Centre of “rushing
  the law through Parliament within 14 hours”.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The total annual outlay for the scheme is estimated at
  approximately ₹1.51 lakh crore (including State shares), with the
  Centre’s share projected at ₹95,692 crore.

• This represents the highest Budget Estimate allocation ever made
  for a rural employment programme in India – 40% of the total
  budget of the Department of Rural Development.

• For 2026-27, the Department of Rural Development’s budget is ₹2.2
  lakh crore.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act retains provisions for biometric authentication for
  transactions, geospatial technology for planning and
  monitoring, and mobile application-based dashboards for real-time
  tracking.

• Section 20 of the Act reinforces social audits conducted by
  Gram Sabhas, ensuring community oversight, transparency and
  inclusion.

• However, civil society groups like LibTech India have argued that
  the Act has no new provisions to mitigate corruption and that
  technology should not become the “sole gateway to employment,
  wages, or accountability”.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The new VB-GRAMG Act removes the mandatory universalization
  clause that was present in MGNREGA (which required the Act to be
  extended to the whole of rural India within five years).

• Under Section 5(1) of the VB-GRAMG Act, employment shall be
  provided only “in such rural areas in the State as may be
  notified by the Central Government”.

• Critics argue that this shift empowers the Central Government
  to indefinitely exclude some rural areas from the employment
  guarantee, fundamentally altering the character of the right to work.

VB-GRAMG Act


• In December 2025, the Punjab Assembly unanimously passed a
  resolution against the Centre’s move to replace MGNREGA.

• The resolution argued that VB-GRAMG converts a demand-driven
  scheme into a norm-based scheme tied to centrally-determined
  budgets instead of labour demand, potentially converting the
  “guarantee” into a budget-capped provision.

• Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, however, termed the special
  session of the Punjab Assembly “against the federal spirit of our
  Constitution” because a state legislature cannot reject a law passed
  by Parliament.

India Rejects COA Award


• On May 16, 2026, India categorically rejected the “so-called award”
  issued by the Court of Arbitration (CoA) at The Hague regarding the
  Indus Waters Treaty (IWT).

• The award reportedly concerned “maximum pondage” at Indian
  hydroelectric projects on the Indus river system.

• India reiterated that it does not recognise the tribunal as legitimately
  constituted, and that any proceeding, award or decision issued by it
  is “null and void”.

India Rejects COA Award
Timeline –

• On September 19, 1960, India and Pakistan signed the Indus
  Waters Treaty in Karachi after nearly nine years of negotiations, with
  mediation by the World Bank.

    ➢ Eastern rivers (India): Sutlej, Beas, and Ravi. India
     enjoys “unrestricted use” of waters from these rivers.

    ➢ Western rivers – (Pakistan): Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab.

• India retains limited rights on the Western rivers for hydropower
  generation, non-consumptive use, and irrigation under
  specified conditions.

India Rejects COA Award


• In 2016, Pakistan unilaterally approached the Court of Arbitration,
  challenging the design of India’s Kishenganga (330
  MW) and Ratle (850 MW) hydroelectric projects on the Chenab
  river.

• Simultaneously, India requested the appointment of a Neutral
  Expert under the treaty’s dispute resolution mechanism.

• This led to the unprecedented situation of parallel proceedings –
  both a Neutral Expert and a Court of Arbitration examining the same
  set of issues, which India has consistently argued violates the treaty.

India Rejects COA Award


• In 2022, the World Bank appointed both a Neutral Expert (Michel
  Lino) and a Chairman of the Court of Arbitration (Prof. Sean
  D. Murphy) simultaneously.

• India challenged this decision, arguing that the treaty does not
  provide for parallel proceedings and that the technical questions
  fall within the Neutral Expert’s mandate.

• Pakistan, however, continued to pursue the arbitration route, and the
  CoA was formally constituted in January 2023.

India Rejects COA Award

• On January 25, 2023, India issued its first notice to Pakistan
  seeking modification of the treaty under Article XII(3) , citing
  Pakistan’s alleged intransigence in implementing the treaty’s
  provisions.

• On August 30, 2024, India issued a second notice seeking “review
  and modification” of the treaty, highlighting fundamental and
  unforeseen changes in circumstances as grounds for
  renegotiation.

• Pakistan did not respond positively to either notice, and India has
  since reiterated its position that the treaty must be updated to reflect
  contemporary realities.

India Rejects COA Award

• On April 22, 2025, the Pahalgam terror attack killed 26 Indian
  tourists in Jammu and Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-based terrorist
  groups.

• India suspended Treaty and shut down the Baglihar and Salal
  dams on the Chenab River – halting nearly 90% of the Chenab’s
  water and curbing water flow to Pakistan’s Punjab.

• The government also increased storage at the Kishanganga Dam
  on the Jhelum River and announced plans to revive six long-stalled
  hydroelectric projects in Jammu and Kashmir (including the 1,856
  MW Sawalkot project).

India Rejects COA Award


• Under the treaty, India can build “run-of-the-river” hydroelectric
  plants on the Western rivers, which generate electricity without
  significantly storing water.

• The Kishenganga (330 MW) and Ratle (850 MW) projects on
  the Chenab river have been the primary points of contention.

• Pakistan claims these projects violate treaty parameters by enabling
  potential manipulation of river flows; India maintains they are fully
  compliant.

India Rejects COA Award

Three tier mechanism –

• The Permanent Indus Commission is the 1st tier of the treaty’s
  grievance redressal mechanism, consisting of one Commissioner
  appointed by each country.

• The Commissioners meet regularly, conduct field inspections, and
  endeavor to resolve minor technical queries or operational disputes
  through mutual consensus.

• If no agreement is reached, the matter is escalated and deemed
  a “difference” .

India Rejects COA Award


• For technical differences that the PIC cannot resolve, either party can
  approach the World Bank to appoint an independent Neutral Expert
  which is the 2nd tier.

• The Neutral Expert’s mandate is strictly limited to reviewing factual
  and technical engineering questions, and the decision
  is binding on both parties.

• In January 2025, Neutral Expert Michel Lino ruled that he
  is “competent” to decide on the Kishenganga and Ratle disputes –
  a ruling India has welcomed.

India Rejects COA Award


• If the issues involve broader legal or treaty interpretations, or if a
  Neutral Expert determines the matter is beyond its technical purview,
  the difference elevates to a “dispute” .

• At this stage, a seven-member ad hoc arbitral tribunal (the
  Court of Arbitration) is formed at The Hague – Court of Arbitration
  which is 3rd tier.

• This is the highest legal authority under the treaty, but India
  argues it has been invoked illegally in the present case.

India Rejects COA Award


Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) –

• The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) is an
  intergovernmental organisation established in 1899 at the First
  Hague Peace Conference to facilitate arbitration between states.

• It is headquartered at The Hague, Netherlands, and acts as
  the secretariat to the Court of Arbitration under the IWT.

• The PCA does not decide disputes; it provides administrative support
  to arbitral tribunals, including the CoA in the India-Pakistan water
  dispute.

India Rejects COA Award


• Article IX of the IWT establishes the treaty’s graded dispute
  resolution mechanism: (1) bilateral discussions (PIC), (2) neutral
  expert (technical differences), (3) court of arbitration (legal disputes).

• Annexure F details the Neutral Expert appointment procedure and
  the World Bank’s role; Paragraph 7 establishes the Expert’s
  competence to decide technical differences.

• Article XII(3) of the IWT provides for the modification of the treaty
  by a duly ratified agreement between the two governments,
  ensuring that any changes require mutual consent.

India Rejects COA Award

Recent News –

• On May 15, 2026, the Court of Arbitration reportedly issued a
  “supplemental award” concerning “maximum pondage” at Indian
  hydroelectric projects on the Indus river system.

• This award is an extension of the CoA’s August 2025 “Award on
  Issues of General Interpretation”, which had ruled largely in
  Pakistan’s favor.

• No official communication of the award is publicly available on the
  PCA website, as India has refused to participate in the proceedings
  from the beginning.

India Rejects COA Award


• On May 16, 2026, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal
  stated: “India categorically rejects the present so-called award, just
  as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements of the illegally
  constituted CoA.”

• He reiterated that India has never recognised the establishment of
  this “so-called” Court of Arbitration, calling it “illegally
  constituted”.

• Jaiswal also confirmed that India’s decision to keep the Indus
  Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force.

India Rejects COA Award


• The CoA concluded a three-day hearing on April 28, 2026, on
  Pakistan’s request for interim measures and on the status of the
  Treaty itself.

• A PCA press release noted that Pakistan was represented by Acting
  Co-Agent Syed Haider Shah along with counsel including Sir Daniel
  Bethlehem KC and Prof. Philippa Webb KC.

• India did not respond to an invitation to participate and did
  not appear at the hearing, consistent with its boycott of the entire
  CoA process.

India Rejects COA Award


• In August 2025, the CoA issued an “Award on Issues of General
  Interpretation” that ruled largely in Pakistan’s favour.

• The award restricted how India calculates permissible pondage for
  run-of-river plants and narrowed the design latitude available
  under the Treaty.

• India rejected this award as well, and the May 2026
  supplemental award is an extension of the same illegal proceedings.

India Rejects COA Award


• Following the decision to place the treaty in abeyance, India wrote to
  Neutral Expert Michel Lino requesting a pause in his
  proceedings on the Ratle and Kishenganga hydropower disputes.

• The request was based on the Union government’s position that the
  treaty itself is in abeyance, and therefore proceedings under it
  should also be suspended.

• The Neutral Expert, Michel Lino is moving forward with proceedings,
  with a final decision expected by January 2027, and Pakistan
  has opposed India’s request to pause the proceedings.

India Rejects COA Award


• India’s decision to keep the IWT in abeyance is based on
  the principle of material breach under international law – a
  fundamental violation of the treaty by one party that justifies the
  other party’s suspension of performance.

• The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
  (1969) recognizes that a material breach of a treaty by one party
  entitles the other party to suspend the operation of the treaty in
  whole or in part.

• India argues that Pakistan’s support for cross-border terrorism
  constitutes a material breach of the treaty’s foundational premises,
  justifying the suspension of India’s obligations.

India Rejects COA Award


• Pakistan has accused India of violating the IWT and has consistently
  sought international arbitration to resolve the disputes over the
  Kishenganga and Ratle projects.

• The CoA’s rulings have largely favoured Pakistan, but India has
  rejected them on the ground that the CoA itself is “illegally
  constituted” .

• The dispute remains unresolved, with both sides entrenched in their
  legal positions, and no clear pathway to a negotiated settlement
  currently in sight.
